title: How the Grid Keeps the Lights On
subtitle: From spinning magnets to your wall socket
logline: Electricity is made, stepped up, shipped and balanced every second.

scenes.heading: Spinning magnets
scenes.concept: Generators turn rotation into alternating current.
sentences: Every power plant ends the same way, with a magnet spinning inside coils of copper wire.
Each turn pushes electrons back and forth sixty times a second.
scenes.visual_idea: A generator cutaway spins up while its output wave grows and a frequency readout climbs to 60 Hz.

scenes.heading: Boost the voltage
scenes.concept: High voltage means low current, so long lines lose less.
sentences: A transformer next to the plant raises the voltage to 400,000 volts.
Higher voltage means less current, so the long lines waste far less energy as heat.
scenes.visual_idea: Flux circulates in a transformer core with few primary and many secondary turns, then current streams down a cool high-voltage line.

scenes.heading: Balance every second
scenes.concept: Supply must match demand or the frequency drifts.
sentences: When a city switches on its kettles, demand jumps ahead of supply.
The frequency sags below 60 Hz until plants open their throttles and catch up.
scenes.visual_idea: City lights brighten, the supply-demand see-saw tips, and the frequency needle dips to 59.95 Hz before recovering.
